name: Rosa Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in software engineering in Valencia, and I share a flat near the campus with my friend Marta, who does biology. Weekdays are lectures from nine, then programming labs, and on Tuesdays and Thursdays I'm in the robotics club building a small line-following robot. On Saturday mornings I tutor two teenagers in maths for pocket money. My parents pay for everything, my mum teaches primary school and my dad works for the regional government, so I'm lucky and I know it. I use a chatbot sometimes when a compile error makes no sense, but I check what it tells me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with five pictures of the next few years. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief for a lot of people, and also a bit funny after all the headlines. At the robotics club we'd probably joke that our line-following robot is the only AI that matters. I'd tell friends to keep learning the basics anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine. I chose software because I like building things, and a calmer market means my first job is more likely to exist. The thing is, I'd still worry that companies keep squeezing junior pay while saying it's all just normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly. Finish my labs, keep the tutoring on Saturdays, and apply for a summer internship at a logistics company near Valencia port. I'd keep using the chatbot only for the compile errors that waste my evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Plain and boring calm, which is nice. I'd still think about my parents' retirement a bit, because prices keep going up whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said junior pay still worries you. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said junior pay still worries you. Why? My cousin Nacho got a first job at a consultancy for less than the minimum they'd advertised. They said it was market rate, and he had no one to argue with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you do about it? I'd probably join a graduate union or at least ask on forums what the real starting pay is. Information is the only power a first-year really has.

say: I'd say it's a relief for many people, and a bit **funny** after the headlines.
I'd tell friends to keep learning the **basics** anyway.
think: I'd be fine, because a calmer market makes my **first job** more likely.
I'd still worry companies **squeeze junior pay** and call it normal.
do: Keep up labs and my Saturday **tutoring** job.
Apply for a summer **internship** at a logistics firm near Valencia port.
Use the chatbot only for **compile errors**.
feel: **Calm**, plain and boring, with a little worry about prices.
S0.quote: Information is the only power a first-year really has.
fieldNote: Her calm rests on **family money** and on a market that stays normal.
Her worry is **junior pay**, learned from her cousin Nacho's consultancy job.
She believes in sharing real pay information as a fairness tool.

steps.text: Apply for a summer internship at a logistics firm in Valencia
Keep tutoring two teenagers in maths on Saturdays
Ask graduate forums what real starting pay is

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we need to talk about who benefits. At the robotics club, I'd say software is the first place it lands because it's a thinking job. I'd say it online carefully, because I don't want to sound like I'm panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think the first jobs it takes are the ones I'm aiming for: junior programmers writing small features and tests. Companies might hire three juniors instead of ten. I'd be competing with my whole cohort of about 200 for fewer seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools properly, not just for errors. I'd learn how to review code that a machine writes, because that's a skill people will still need. I'd also add a robotics or hardware module, since hands-on work changes more slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some control. It's like a big exam that's two years away: you can see it and you can study. I'd feel better if the university taught this openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to review machine code. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd learn to review machine code. How? I'd read open-source projects and fix small bugs on weekends. A senior from my club, Joaquín, did that and got an internship because a maintainer vouched for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gains most from all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who gains most from all this? The companies who own the models, and the people who already have capital. I'd want the gains shared through shorter weeks or retraining paid for by the companies that own the models.

say: I'd say it's real and we need to talk about **who benefits**.
I'd say software is where it lands first.
think: The jobs it takes first are the **junior programmer** ones I'm aiming for.
Firms might hire **three juniors** instead of ten.
do: Learn to **review machine-written code** by fixing bugs in open-source projects.
Use AI tools properly, not just for errors.
feel: **Anxious**, but with some control, like an exam two years away.
S1.quote: I'd want the gains shared through shorter weeks or retraining paid for by the companies that own the models.
fieldNote: She moves from occasional AI use to **deliberate skill-building**.
Believes gains should be shared, a progressive view stated plainly.
Joaquín's open-source route gives her a concrete model to copy.

steps.text: Fix small bugs in open-source projects on weekends
Add a robotics module to second-year choices
Ask the dean for an open course on AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need governments to act this month: public funds for people who lose work, strict rules on who owns the models, and shorter weeks. I'd say it loudly, even if it feels like shouting into the wind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my degree could be obsolete before I graduate. The whole point of software is thinking work, and that's the first thing AGI does better and cheaper. I'd graduate into almost no entry-level jobs and no time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in university and use the time to get hands-on skills. I'd ask my parents if I could switch to electronics or mechatronics, since robots come later in 2031. I'd also join the student union and sign every petition, and I'd try to volunteer at a repair cafe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd think about it in bed, and I'd talk to Marta at one in the morning. Mostly I'd feel angry that nobody asked us before it happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really change degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you really change degree? I'd think hard about it. Switching costs a year, but a year is cheap compared to a degree that has no jobs. My mum would back me, but my dad would say wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents that night? I'd say don't panic about the money, we'll sort it. And I'd be lying, because I'd be panicking myself.

say: I'd say governments must act now: **public funds**, rules on who owns the models, shorter weeks.
I'd say it **loudly**, even if it feels futile.
think: My degree could be **obsolete** before I graduate, because software is thinking work.
I'd graduate into almost **no entry-level jobs**.
do: Ask my parents about switching to **mechatronics**, since robots come later.
Join the student union and sign every **petition**.
Volunteer at a **repair cafe** to build hands-on skills.
feel: **Alarmed**, angry that nobody asked us before it happened.
S2.quote: A year is cheap compared to a degree that has no jobs.
fieldNote: She turns to **policy demands** and hands-on skills at once.
Her dad's wait-and-see against her urgency shows a split at home.
Admits she'd hide her panic from her parents.

steps.text: Ask my parents about switching to mechatronics next year
Join the student union and sign petitions for public funds
Volunteer at the repair cafe on Saturdays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we can still push for change if we start now. I'd say it to the robotics club and our parents' generation, because they vote. I'd also say people shouldn't wait for companies to be kind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I have enough time to be useful. I'd graduate in 2030 and the AGI date is 2031, so I'd be entering at the worst moment. But I'd have a few years to learn things that aren't pure thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI tools daily so I'm not left behind, and I'd choose electives in robotics and embedded systems. I'd also build a small portfolio with real projects, and apply for internships at hardware firms. And I'd save my tutoring money in a separate account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Five years feels like a storm forecast: you can't stop it, but you can pack. I'd still wake up some nights thinking about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save your tutoring money. Why separate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd save your tutoring money. Why separate? In case I need to retrain or move. My parents pay for now, but I don't know if they'll have the same income if things change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you want from the university? Courses that mix software with hardware, and honest talks from people already losing work. Not the usual careers fair with free pens.

say: I'd say five years means we can still push for **change** if we start now.
I'd say people shouldn't wait for companies to be **kind**.
think: I'd graduate in 2030, just before the **2031 date**, the worst moment to enter.
I'd have **time to learn** things that aren't pure thinking work.
do: Use AI tools **daily** and take robotics and embedded-systems electives.
Build a **portfolio** of real projects and apply to hardware firms.
Save tutoring money in a **separate account**.
feel: **Anxious** but steady, like packing for a forecast storm.
S3.quote: Five years feels like a storm forecast: you can't stop it, but you can pack.
fieldNote: Five years moves her from occasional to **daily AI use** with hardware electives.
She worries about her parents' income, not only her own.
Wants honest talks from people already losing work, not careers-fair pens.

steps.text: Choose robotics and embedded systems electives for second year
Build a portfolio of three real projects
Move tutoring money into a separate savings account
Apply to hardware firms for summer internships

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disaster if we don't. I'd tell friends to enjoy their studies but keep their eyes open. And I'd say we should be voting for people who have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I could have a full first decade as an engineer. I'd graduate, work for a few years, maybe get a master's, and have options. It feels like enough time to change direction at least once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take an internship every summer, and use AI tools to learn faster. I'd probably do a master's in robotics to be on the hands-on side. I'd also invest a little each month, even small amounts, in a plain index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I can plan for ten years, and I'm good at plans. What I can't plan for is whether the world around me is fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the world fair enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make the world fair enough? Shared gains, like a shorter week and a public fund so nobody is stranded. If it's only a few firms getting richer, I'd say that's a political failure, not a technical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think your mum would say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you think your mum would say? She'd say teach children kindness and numbers, because machines can't be there in the room. She's already sure primary teaching is safe, and I hope she's right.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if we use it and a disaster if we don't.
I'd say vote for people with a **plan**.
think: I could have a **full first decade** as an engineer.
Ten years is enough to **change direction** at least once.
do: Finish the degree, with an **internship** every summer.
Do a master's in **robotics** to stay on the hands-on side.
Invest a small amount monthly in a plain **index fund**.
feel: **Uneasy** but hopeful, since I'm good at plans.
S4.quote: If it's only a few firms getting richer, I'd say that's a political failure, not a technical one.
fieldNote: Her optimism depends on **fair sharing** of gains.
Her mum's belief that teaching is safe gives her some comfort.
Planning is how she copes, and she links fairness to politics, not to technology.

steps.text: Take a summer internship every year of the degree
Apply for a master's in robotics
Invest a small amount monthly in an index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because there's no time. The other four give me years to learn and to push for rules, but two years means my degree would be half done and the jobs gone. What would help is public support for people who lose work and a way to switch courses without paying twice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say that people my age aren't only scared, we're also angry and a bit hopeful. We want someone to explain what's happening without selling us something.

headlineQuote: We want someone to explain what's happening without selling us something.
portrait: Rosa is an 18-year-old **software engineering** student in Valencia, with parents who pay for everything and a Saturday tutoring job.
She uses a chatbot **sometimes** and checks its answers, and she adapts when change is proven.
Progressive, she wants **shared gains**: shorter weeks, public funds and open information about pay.
In fast AGI she turns alarmed and political; with ten years she plans a **robotics** master's.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, since her degree would be half done and the jobs gone.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **public support** for people who lose work and a way to switch courses without paying twice.
